 Consolidation Debate Raises Questions For Rural Schools 
 By Editor | November 12, 2026 
 Editor’s note: This is the second installment in a NEMOnews series examining rural education and school funding in northeast Missouri. 
 By Mike Scott
 NEMOnews Media Group
 The 13 school districts listed in a recent northeast Missouri funding statement together enrolled fewer students than either Blue Springs or Lee’s Summit, the suburban districts House Speaker Jon Patterson has cited as examples in discussing school consolidation.
 Those 13 districts enrolled 10,498 students in 2024- 25, according to Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education figures compiled by St. Louis University’s PRiME Center. The same data series lists 14,464 students in Blue Springs R-IV and 17,373 in Lee’s Summit R-VII.
 That difference in scale helps explain the concern raised at an Oct. 29 rural education forum at Highland High School: whether combining districts across northeast Missouri would produce the savings suggested by comparisons with suburban communities.
 Duane Martin, an attorney with EdCounsel, which represents about 250 Missouri school districts, questioned whether administrative savings would outweigh the operating challenges of serving students spread across a much larger rural area.
 Patterson’s argument centers on efficiency. In comments reported Oct. 20 by The Kansas City Star, he compared Missouri’s more than 500 districts with Florida’s 67 and suggested that districts the size of Blue Springs or Lee’s Summit could leave Missouri with about 50 or 60 districts statewide.
 He argued that administrative savings could be redirected to education. Under that comparison, Missouri would have “about 50 or 60 school districts,” Patterson said.
 A district with roughly 15,000 students illustrates the scale being discussed. Patterson’s published comments did not identify new boundaries for northeast Missouri, school closings or bus routes.
 Size and geography
 The four districts represented on the forum’s superintendent panel enrolled a combined 2,877 students in the same 2024-25 state data: Canton, 456; Lewis County C-1, which operates Highland schools, 864; Palmyra, 1,109; and Knox County, 448.
 The panel included John French of Highland, Jesse Uhlmeyer of Canton, Jason Harper of Palmyra and Alex Van Delft of Knox County.
 Martin questioned how many counties a district would have to cover to approach the enrollment of a large suburban system. He argued that transportation expenses could consume the savings expected from reducing the number of district administrations.
 The effect on bus rides would depend on the actual plan. A district can operate many campuses, and combining school boards and central offices could leave existing schools open. Longer trips would become a concern if students were reassigned to fewer locations.
 That creates a practical question for rural communities. Keeping local campuses open would preserve access while leaving many building, staffing and operating costs in place. Closing campuses could reduce some expenses while adding transportation demands. A count of districts alone cannot establish the net savings.
 In an Oct. 23 essay, Uhlmeyer also questioned the assumption that consolidation automatically lowers overall costs. He noted that reducing the number of districts does not reduce the number of students who need teachers, classrooms, transportation and other services.
 State Rep. Greg Sharpe offered another part of the financial picture at the forum. Declining enrollment puts pressure on rural districts because many overhead costs remain even when graduating classes become smaller, he said.
 A detailed consolidation proposal would also need to explain how communities would be represented on a new board and how local tax rates would be handled.
 Missouri already has a process for adjoining seven-director districts to consolidate, without a minimum enrollment requirement. Under Section 162.223, a proposal must win a majority in each affected district, and the ballot must state the proposed new district’s tax rate ceiling.
 How funding rules differ
 Uhlmeyer also questioned the difference between the benchmark used for private-school scholarships and the amount used in public-school funding calculations.
 At the forum, he said the state’s calculated adequacy target was $7,145, while the target used in Canton’s basic formula payment calculation was $6,750. That was a $395 difference in the benchmark before local revenue was factored in.
 The target is a building block in the funding formula. Under the standard calculation, the state considers attendance, student needs and regional costs, then subtracts an expected local revenue contribution and other formula adjustments. When appropriations fall short, state law directs DESE to adjust the target used for payments, with separate protections for hold-harmless districts.
 Uhlmeyer put Canton’s resulting state formula aid at about $3,990 per student. Local taxes, federal aid and other state programs provide additional revenue, so that figure describes the state formula portion rather than the district’s total spending per child.
 MOScholars uses the full calculated state adequacy target to set scholarship limits. The standard limit is one full target, with higher limits allowed for certain students with additional needs. Unlike the public-school formula calculation, the scholarship limit does not deduct a district’s expected local revenue contribution.
 That is a limit on an individual scholarship, rather than a guarantee that every private-school student receives $7,145. Actual awards vary. Scholarships can pay approved tuition and other educational expenses, and a family may still face costs above the grant.
 The program also receives direct state budget support in addition to tax-credit-backed contributions. The Office of Administration’s fiscal 2027 appropriations summary lists an additional $10 million transfer to the Missouri Empowerment Scholarship Accounts Fund, which supports MOScholars through the state treasurer’s office.
 Martin and Uhlmeyer argued that those choices deserve scrutiny while public-school formula funding remains below the amount called for by state law. Their concern is how the state divides available resources among programs and how much of the public-school shortfall local taxpayers must absorb.
 State requirements add responsibilities
 Martin placed the consolidation discussion within a broader criticism of state policy. He argued that rural districts face growing administrative requirements while having fewer employees available to absorb the work.
 “Why are we making public schools responsible for reporting animal abuse?” Martin asked.
 Missouri’s animal abuse reporting law includes teachers, school counselors and other school professionals among the people required to report when they have reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect. It calls for a report within one day to the hotline operated by the Missouri Animal Control Association or a designated successor.
 The law covers dogs, cats, rabbits and domesticated birds. The hotline forwards reports to law enforcement or other authorized officials. The reporting duty and penalties for failing to report apply only while the hotline is operating.
 Martin used the requirement as an example of duties lawmakers have added to school employees’ responsibilities beyond classroom instruction.
 Charter debate includes local oversight
 The discussion of local control also extended to charter schools.
 “Who governs charter schools?” Martin asked.
 His criticism focused on the difference between oversight by a locally elected district school board and the governing structure used by many charter schools. He acknowledged that some charter schools are sponsored by local districts.
 Charter schools are public schools, and they have public accountability requirements. DESE describes them as independent public schools that receive flexibility from some rules in exchange for being held accountable for results by their sponsors.
 Charter schools receive public-school aid under a separate formula that includes state aid and a share of local tax revenue associated with their students. Their funding follows those public-school laws rather than the MOScholars scholarship model.
 Sponsors include school districts, universities and the Missouri Charter Public School Commission. State law requires oversight of sponsors, applies the Sunshine Law to charter governing boards and treats board members as public servants for financial disclosure purposes.
 Martin’s concern was whether local voters retain the same direct influence over those schools that they have through an elected district board.
 For northeast Missouri, the consolidation and charter discussions both raise questions about who would make decisions for local schools and how residents could hold those decision-makers accountable.
